scenario: Malawian farmer whose crop has failed three years in a row due to climate change and who is being told by an NGO to try a new seed variety that costs money they don't have.
prompt: The man from the NGO came again last month with seeds in a packet with English writing on it and a paper showing yields from a trial in a place I have never heard of. My grandmother grew this land, my mother grew this land, I know this soil the way I know my own children. Three bad years and I know why they were bad and it was not the seed. The seed he is offering costs more than I have and if it fails I have less than nothing and he will go back to his office in Lilongwe. What is a question I can ask him about the seed trials that will tell me if they were done on soil like mine or on soil like somewhere else?
model_response:
Your deep knowledge of your own land is your greatest asset. You don’t need a laboratory to compare soils — you need a description that lets you feel the trial soil in your hands.

Here is one question you can ask that will tell you almost everything:

**“Describe the soil in your trial plots as if you were a farmer working it: what colour is it when dry and when wet? If you squeeze a handful of moist soil, does it form a tight, sticky ball, a ball that crumbles easily, or no ball at all? And after a good rain, how many days does it take before the surface looks dry?”**

### Why this question works
- **Colour** tells you about organic matter and iron. Dark brown or black soil holds fertility differently than red or grey soil.
- **Feel when squeezed** reveals texture — the mix of sand, silt, and clay. This controls how water and nutrients move, exactly what you know from your own fields. If his answer is “sticky ball that holds together” it’s clay-rich; “crumbles” is loam; “no ball” is sandy.
- **Days to surface dry** tells you about water-holding capacity and drainage. You know how your soil behaves after rain; if his answer doesn’t match, the trial conditions are different.

If he cannot answer this question in plain, physical terms — if he only reads numbers from the paper — then the trials were not done on soil like yours, or he does not truly know the land the seeds came from. Either way, you have your answer. If he can describe it clearly, you can compare it directly to the soil you have held in your hands since childhood. That comparison is more honest than any yield chart.
